A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same federated Q-learning work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete Appendices A–G support a reliable comparison.

before.justification: Section 6 and Appendix G report original Q-learning simulations in homogeneous and heterogeneous maze environments, using five independent runs.

after.justification: Section 6 and Appendix G report original maze simulations, including additional time-decaying stepsize and sensitivity results.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 retains the same local Q-learning updates, periodic averaging, initialization, and global learning target. The two-phase stepsize strategy already appears in v1; v2 evaluates additional schedules without introducing a new method component.

E1.justification: Both versions use randomly generated 5×5 mazes with 25 states and four actions under homogeneous and heterogeneous transitions. The additional stepsize, synchronization, and horizon experiments retain this task coverage.

E2.justification: The evaluated comparisons remain single-phase versus two-phase federated Q-learning and its configuration variants. No additional competing RL algorithm is evaluated. Table 1 retains the same related-work membership.

E3.justification: Section 6 changes the reported agent count from 5 to 20. V2 additionally evaluates four time-decaying schedules, including 1/sqrt(t+1), (c+1)/(t+c) with c=10, 1/(t+1), and 1/(t+1)^0.7, and introduces synchronization-period and training-horizon sweeps. These substantially expand the experimental settings while retaining the maze construction and error metric.

E4.justification: V1 mentions time-varying stepsize experiments but does not display their results. V2 Figure 4b–e tests whether two-phase training remains beneficial under four decay schedules. New Figures 6–7 examine synchronization sensitivity with a decaying stepsize and final-error dependence on training horizon, substantially extending the convergence analyses.

E5.justification: Both versions specify five independent runs, mean curves, and shading representing one standard deviation above and below the mean. The added results do not introduce a different uncertainty-reporting procedure.

E6.justification: V2 adds findings of two-phase benefits across four decay schedules, worsening convergence with larger synchronization periods under decaying stepsizes, and decreasing final error with larger horizons. Existing tolerance-crossing results also change: the 10% crossing for phase-1 stepsize 0.9 changes from 16502 to 16198 iterations, and the 3% crossing for 0.05 changes from 16687 to 15998 (v1 Figure 6; v2 Figure 8). The changed reported agent count prevents interpreting these as same-setting performance gains.

T1.justification: Theorem 1 adds E−1≤1/(Kλ) and simplifies its bound; Corollary 1 revises the admissible range and discount-factor dependence. New Corollary 2 derives explicit sample-complexity regimes. Theorem 2 incorporates horizon and E≥2 restrictions from v1 Appendix F and introduces explicit reward cases, including equal rewards. Its discount-factor scaling was already present in v1's proof.

C1.justification: V1 emphasizes partial speedup of sampling error and slowdown with multiple local updates. V2 centers its abstract and contributions on a threshold in K(E−1) separating linear-speedup and heterogeneity-dominated sample-complexity regimes, and explicitly states discount- and reward-dependent lower-bound claims. The contribution list also extends two-phase benefits to time-decaying schedules.

C2.justification: New Remarks 3–4 explain communication savings and conditional linear speedup. New Section 5.3 discusses why constant-stepsize proofs do not directly cover time-varying schedules and labels comparable asymptotic behavior as a conjecture. V2 also adds conjectured mechanisms for the two phases and explains why larger synchronization periods may require smaller or faster-decaying stepsizes.

D1.justification: V2 specifies the newly evaluated decay formulas and c=10. Conversely, its simplified Figure 4 legend removes the per-schedule phase-switch times supplied in v1's legend; only the highlighted t0=5550 case remains in the prose. These are limited additions and losses of reproducibility information.

R1.justification: V2 adds a Multi-Agent RL discussion citing Christianos et al., Yu et al., and Zhong et al., and discusses Salgia and Chi's sample–communication tradeoff work. A new technical-comparison subsection substantially expands positioning against Woo, Zhang, and Wang, emphasizing vanishing error, heterogeneity effects, and lower-bound novelty. Zhang's publication updates concern an already cited work.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and much existing prose remain. V2 makes targeted rewrites to the abstract, contributions, related work, and experimental discussion, improves proof signposting, adds Section 5.3, reorganizes Appendix G, and updates author and publication information.

P2.justification: Table 1 moves from the appendix into Related Work. Figure 3 changes from four panels in one row to a 2×2 arrangement; Figure 4 moves into Appendix G and expands from one to five panels. New Figures 6–7 are added, the former tolerance figure becomes Figure 8, and legends and journal page formatting are extensively revised.

improvement.justification: V2 provides useful sample-complexity regimes, clearer scope discussion, and additional convergence checks. However, v1 Appendix F uses rewards in general position, whereas v2 Theorem 2 and Appendix F introduce a positive lower bound for equal rewards. For equal nonzero rewards, the paper's own recurrence gives error proportional to [1−(1−γ)λ]^T for a fixed positive stepsize, contradicting that 1/T lower bound. This problem in the revised theory coexists with substantial explanatory and empirical gains, preventing a reliable net-quality judgment.
